slides.title: Friendship questions you'd never ask out loud

slides.q: How do I tell a friend I can't be their therapist?
slides.a: Lead with care: "I love you and want to support you, but I can't help with this the way you deserve." Then suggest a next step, like talking to a professional, and offer what you can do, like regular check-ins. Setting that limit protects the friendship from burnout on both sides.

slides.q: Is it weird to have a friend way older than me?
slides.a: Not at all. Friendships across ages can be some of the best ones, because you get different perspectives, advice, and life experience. Lots of people have close friends 10, 20, or even 30 years apart. If you enjoy each other and the friendship feels respectful, the age gap is just a fun detail.

slides.q: How do I deal with a friend who always one-ups me?
slides.a: One-upping often comes from insecurity or wanting to relate, not from trying to make you feel small. You can gently name it: "I really want you to hear this one, can we stay on my thing for a sec?" If it keeps happening, it's okay to share less with them and more with people who listen.

slides.q: Is it okay to not invite everyone to my birthday?
slides.a: Yes. You're allowed to celebrate the way you want, whether that's a big party or dinner with three people. Keeping it small isn't a rejection of everyone else. Just try not to post a ton of photos where left-out friends will see, and maybe plan something separate with others you care about.

slides.q: How do I stay close with a friend who just had a baby?
slides.a: Show up in low-pressure ways: text without expecting a quick reply, drop off food, or offer to visit for an hour. Ask about them, not just the baby. Their time and energy will be limited for a while, and that's not a sign they care less. Keep reaching out. It means a lot.
